A change is verified by a command run after the final edit, and by nothing else. Output quoted from the plan, from an earlier step's report, or from a run that happened before your last edit says nothing about the code as it stands now. Run it yourself, in this step.

Rerun the command that failed, whole. Running one test file when the failing command was the suite proves nothing about the suite. Capture the status with `<command>; echo "exit=$?"` so the exit code is in the text you read.

A success report contains three things: the exact command, its exit status, and the last lines it printed. Without all three, do not write fixed, resolved, passing or works.

If anything was edited after your most recent run, the state is unverified. Write "unverified: edited after the last run", then rerun.

If the rerun fails, that is the outcome, and reporting it is this step done. Quote the new output verbatim, including the parts identical to the previous output: identical output is evidence that the edit changed nothing.

If the command cannot run here, because a dependency, service or network is missing, name the exact command and quote the error that blocked it. "Not verified: running X printed Y" is a report the run above can act on. "Should now work" is not.
skills.prevents: Without it the model makes an edit, does not rerun anything, and reports "fixed" on the strength of its own reasoning — so the run above accepts an unverified change as done and the overnight loop advances on a false premise.

skills.name: run-the-projects-gate
skills.body:
---
name: run-the-projects-gate
description: Use when the task involves running the project's tests, lint, or any check command.
---

# Run the gate the project already has

Find the project's own check command before running anything. Read these files in this order and stop at the first one that names a command: Makefile (a test, check or ci target), package.json (the scripts block), pyproject.toml or tox.ini, CONTRIBUTING.md, README.md, and finally .github/workflows/*.yml. From a workflow file take the literal text of the run: line of the test step, never the whole job. Run the command you found verbatim, from the directory its file lives in.

Do not invent a command. `pytest -q` where the project runs `make test` is a different gate: it can skip a lint stage, drop an integration marker, or load a different config, and it can pass while the real gate fails.

Report four things: the command as one copy-pasteable line, the file and line number you took it from, its exit code, and the last 20 lines it printed, quoted rather than summarised. Exit code 0 is the only thing that counts as passing.

If none of those files names a command, say so and list the files you actually read. You may then run one obvious default (`pytest`, `npm test`), but call it a fallback gate, not the project gate, in every sentence that reports its result.

If the gate never starts (no such target, a missing dependency, an import error before the first test ran), that is not a failing suite. Report that the gate did not run, quote the error, and report no test result at all.
skills.prevents: A step invents its own check command (bare `pytest -q`), gets a green result from a narrower gate than the project's real one, and reports the project as passing.

skills.name: sample-size-floor
skills.body:
---
name: sample-size-floor
description: Use when a conclusion rests on counts, a comparison or a small dataset.
---

# Say when the counts cannot carry the claim

Write the denominator beside every comparison before you interpret it: A 12/50, B 15/50; or 3 of 5 reruns passed after the fix, 1 of 5 before. Then apply these rules.

Fewer than about thirty observations in the smaller group: report both counts and stop. Do not call either side better, faster, or fixed.

Swing the gap to test it. Move two or three items from one group to the other on paper and recompute. If the direction flips, the gap is noise, and you say so.

For a proportion out of n the rough margin is 1/sqrt(n). At n=100 that is about ten points, so a four-point difference at n=100 is not a difference.

Sub-groups are where this goes wrong. A total of 5,000 can contain a cell of 11. Report the row count of every cell you drew a conclusion from, not just the total.

Zero events is its own case. 0/40 does not mean the rate is zero. It means the rate is under roughly 7% and nothing narrower is available from these rows.

The honest output is a result, not a failure. Write: direction B higher, 15/50 versus 12/50, not conclusive at this n. Give the counts and the direction, and refuse the ranking.
skills.prevents: Declaring a winner or a trend from a handful of rows - a four-point gap at n=100, a sub-group of 11 inside a headline n of 5,000, or reading 0/40 as a zero rate.

skills.name: stack-trace-names-the-victim
skills.body:
---
name: stack-trace-names-the-victim
description: Use when a traceback or stack trace is supplied with the task.
---

# A stack trace names the victim

The frame where the program crashed is usually where a bad value was used, not where it was made. Editing that file is the most common wrong fix.

Find the crash frame first: in a Python traceback headed "most recent call last" it is the bottom entry; in a JavaScript or Java stack it is the top. Read outward from there toward your own callers, one frame at a time, asking one question: was the argument this frame received already wrong when it arrived? The first frame that received correct inputs and passed a wrong one onward holds the defect.

Skip any frame whose path contains site-packages, dist-packages, node_modules or a virtualenv, and never edit those files. They are where the wrong value was finally noticed by code strict enough to complain; an edit there is discarded on the next install.

Do not infer the culprit from the exception type. A TypeError says two things did not match; it does not say which one is wrong. Decide by reading the assignment that produced the value. If bash is available, run the failing command and quote its real output; if it is not, quote the line you read. Never claim to have printed something you did not run.

Finish with one line: `defect at <file>:<line>`, naming the frame that received good inputs and passed a bad one on. If no frame did, write `no frame received a wrong argument` and quote the lines inside the crash frame that compute the wrong result. That is a complete answer, not a failure.
skills.prevents: Without it the model treats the last line of the traceback as the defect location and edits that file — often a library file under site-packages or node_modules — instead of the caller that constructed the wrong value, producing a change that is both wrong and discarded on the next install.

skills.name: unverifiable-step-check
skills.body:
---
name: unverifiable-step-check
description: Use when writing or auditing the steps of a plan and each step needs a check that can come back negative.
---

# A step you cannot check is not a step

For each step, write next to it what you would run or open to prove it is done. The check must be able to come back negative: a command with an exit code, a file that either exists or does not, a number compared against a threshold, a document that contains a named section.

These are not checks, and each is a common disguise: reviewed, understood, aligned, improved, refactored for clarity, made more robust. They name a state of mind or a matter of taste, not an observation. Rewrite the step as the artifact it should leave behind, or delete it.

When the real check needs a person or a system you do not have -- a sign-off, a deploy window, a paid API -- do not substitute a proxy check you can run. Write the step as "unverifiable here" and name who or what can verify it. A step marked unverifiable is still usable. A step with a fake check reports success for a reason unrelated to the work, and nobody downstream can see that happen.

Auditing a plan you did not write is the same pass: quote the check each step already carries, or record that it carries none.

Finish with the count: "9 steps, 7 with runnable checks, 2 unverifiable here (t6 needs the vendor sandbox, t9 needs sign-off)". Emit that line even when the numbers are 9, 9 and 0 -- but only once all nine checks are written down next to their steps.
skills.prevents: Steps whose completion is unfalsifiable, and the worse repair of attaching a proxy check that passes for a reason unrelated to the work, which turns an unknown into a reported success.

intake_sources.name: abandoned_change
intake_sources.what_it_reads: `git log --all --grep='^Revert "' --format='%H %ct %s'`, `git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(committerdate:unix)' refs/heads refs/remotes`, and `git rev-list --count main..<ref>`. Verified here: c0c4600 reverts 6fa72e5 ('fix: support MCP SDK 2.x and restore stale static-architecture doc paths'), touching .github/workflows/ci.yml and src/loop_engine/core/mcp_sdk_transport.py; overnight/opencode-step-instances is 1 commit ahead of main; origin/checkpoint/loop-engine-architecture-20260825 is 0 ahead and 118 behind.
intake_sources.signal: Two shapes of one thing — a change that exists and is not in main. First: a revert whose original commit's diff is still absent from HEAD, proved by `git cherry-pick -n <original>` applying cleanly, which means nothing has re-landed it. Second: a ref where `git rev-list --count main..ref` is greater than zero and whose tip subject matches wip/fixup/squash/checkpoint, or whose tip is older than seven days.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: A revert is the engineer recording in the commit graph that a change did not hold — a decision, written down, not an opinion about one. `rev-list --count` is arithmetic over that graph. The same arithmetic is what discards dead work: the checkpoint branch above is 0 ahead, so it carries nothing and is dropped before anyone forms a view about it.
intake_sources.gate_command: Derived, and it must be constructed rather than assumed. For a revert: `git worktree add`, `git cherry-pick <original>`, then run the gate the revert was protecting — for c0c4600 that is CI, because the reverted commit edited ci.yml itself. For an unmerged tip: `git worktree add` at the tip and run the declared gates from head_gate_red. A branch tip whose gates already pass is not a candidate; it is a pull request nobody opened, and the correct output is one line saying so, not a night of work.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: A revert can be a deliberate scope cut rather than a failure, and reapplying it is then unwanted work — require the revert to be under 90 days old and the touched files to still exist, and record the revert's own commit body so a morning reviewer can see the stated reason. A cherry-pick that conflicts means the area moved on and the candidate is stale, not urgent; drop it rather than asking a small model to resolve a semantic conflict overnight. Branch age alone means nothing: stale-and-0-ahead is finished work, which is why the count filter runs before the date filter.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
git log --all --grep='^Revert "' --format='%H %ct %s' | while read -r h ts s; do
  orig=$(git show "$h" | sed -n 's/^ *This reverts commit \([0-9a-f]\{7,\}\).*/\1/p' | head -1)
  [ -z "$orig" ] && continue
  git worktree add -qdf /tmp/rev "$h" 2>/dev/null || continue
  ( cd /tmp/rev && git cherry-pick -n "$orig" >/dev/null 2>&1 ) \
    && echo "UNRELANDED $h reverts $orig :: $s"
  git worktree remove -f /tmp/rev
done
git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads refs/remotes | while read -r b; do
  n=$(git rev-list --count main.."$b" 2>/dev/null) || continue
  [ "${n:-0}" -gt 0 ] && echo "AHEAD $n $b :: $(git log -1 --format='%cr %s' "$b")"
done

intake_sources.name: advisory_reachable
intake_sources.what_it_reads: `npm audit --json --prefix showcase` — verified runnable here, showcase/package.json and showcase/package-lock.json both exist and today's report is 0 vulnerabilities across 22 dependencies — and `pip-audit --format=json` against the environment pyproject.toml declares. GitHub's Dependabot API was tried and is not available for this repository: `gh api repos/alisonjieli-png/loop-engine/dependabot/alerts` returns HTTP 403, 'Dependabot alerts are disabled for this repository.'
intake_sources.signal: An advisory against a package the repository actually imports, with a fixed version published. Reachability is the filter that makes this usable: `git grep -lE '^\s*(import|from) <pkg>'` for Python, the package name in package.json dependencies for Node. An advisory on a transitive package nothing in the tree names is not this project's night.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: The advisory record and the installed version are both facts, and the import is grep over committed source. What is not observed is exploitability, so the candidate must be worded as 'package X is at version Y, advisory Z applies, version W is available' and never as 'the project is vulnerable'. That wording distinction is the whole difference between this source meeting the standard and violating it.
intake_sources.gate_command: Partial, and this is the weakest of the eight — say so in the ranking rather than hiding it. The bump is verifiable: pin the fixed version, re-run npm audit or pip-audit and require that advisory ID to be gone, then re-run the declared gates from head_gate_red and require exit 0. What no gate can prove is that the bump was worth making, so this source must never outrank a red gate and must never be the only candidate proposed for a night.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: On this machine the source currently returns nothing at all: npm audit is clean, Dependabot is disabled, and pip-audit is not installed (`command -v pip-audit` finds nothing, though uv and pip are both present, so installing it is a prerequisite step and not itself a candidate). The risk is therefore padding — reaching for dev-only or unreachable advisories to avoid returning an empty list. Return the empty list. A candidate list padded with advisories nobody would act on teaches the morning reviewer to skim, and then the failing CI step gets skimmed with it.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
npm audit --json --prefix showcase > /tmp/npm.json 2>/dev/null
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, subprocess
vulns = json.load(open('/tmp/npm.json')).get('vulnerabilities', {})
for name, v in vulns.items():
    if not v.get('fixAvailable'):
        continue            # no fix == not a night's work, it is a watch item
    hit = subprocess.run(['git','grep','-lF',name,'--','showcase/package.json','*.mjs','*.js'],
                         capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
    if hit:
        print(v['severity'], name, '->', v['fixAvailable'], '| named in', hit.splitlines()[0])
PY
# Python half is currently inert: `uv tool install pip-audit` must run first,
# and until it does this source reports "python: not checked", not "python: clean".

intake_sources.name: ci_red_step
intake_sources.what_it_reads: gh run list -L 20 --json databaseId,conclusion,headSha,headBranch,workflowName and gh run view <id> --json jobs. Verified working and authenticated here (gh 2.95.0 at /home/username/.local/bin/gh): the five most recent CI runs on main are all conclusion=='failure', and run 34011589193 reports failing steps 'Check local links and section anchors' (job: public documentation) and 'Self-orientation and hardcoding delta gates' (jobs: suite + conformance gates 3.10, 3.11, 3.12). The failing step name is then looked up in the committed .github/workflows/ci.yml to recover its run: block.
intake_sources.signal: A step with conclusion=='failure' on the newest run for a branch that is also failing on the run before it. One red run is a flake; the same step red across consecutive runs, or across all three Python versions of a matrix, is the project's own gate saying the branch is broken and nobody has fixed it.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: GitHub records the step's exit status; the step-name-to-command mapping is read out of a file in the repository. Both halves are facts on disk. Nothing here is a claim by an agent about what it thinks broke, and the failing log text is available verbatim rather than summarised.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes, and this is the best gate of the eight: the workflow's run: block is an acceptance test the project already wrote and already agreed to. For the live example, the step's block is `PYTHONPATH=devtools/src python -m loop_engine_devtools.cli --self-test` followed by the --hardcoding-audit invocation with --allowlist devtools/hardcoding-allowlist.yaml --baseline devtools/hardcoding-ci-baseline.json --fail-on-new high.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: The local reproduction can fail for a different reason than CI's. Running that exact hardcoding-audit line here exits 1 on 'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named loop_engine' at devtools/src/loop_engine_devtools/assurance/hardcoding.py:1225, because CI runs `pip install -e '.[all]'` first and this checkout does not have the package installed. So the candidate must carry CI's failing log excerpt, and the night's first move is to confirm the local error text matches it; a mismatch means the candidate is a local environment defect, which is a different and much smaller job. Separately: do not parse `gh run view --log-failed` for step names — it labels every line 'UNKNOWN STEP'. Use --json jobs.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
for id in $(gh run list -L 20 --json databaseId,conclusion \
      -q '.[]|select(.conclusion=="failure")|.databaseId'); do
  gh run view "$id" --json headSha,jobs -q '.headSha as $s | .jobs[]
     | select(.conclusion=="failure")
     | "\($s) \(.name) :: \(.steps[]|select(.conclusion=="failure")|.name)"'
done | awk -F':: ' '{c[$2]++} END{for (s in c) if (c[s]>1) print c[s], s}'
# each surviving step name -> its run: block in .github/workflows/ci.yml,
# plus `gh run view <id> --log-failed | grep -n "##\[error\]"` for the text.

intake_sources.name: codex_exec_exit
intake_sources.what_it_reads: ~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl — verified present: 43 rollout files, e.g. /home/username/.codex/sessions/2026/09/06/rollout-2026-09-06T01-05-14-01a0751b-3cc3-7981-9cc5-cc56a6d46a64.jsonl (6086 lines). Records with payload.type=='custom_tool_call' and name=='exec' (7795 across the 43 sessions) joined by call_id to payload.type=='custom_tool_call_output', whose output[].text embeds a JSON envelope carrying "label", "exit_code", "wall_time_seconds" and the captured "output". Session cwd comes from the turn_context record (observed value: /home/username/loop-engine). Also ~/.codex/history.jsonl (85 lines) for the session_id -> prompt join.
intake_sources.signal: An exec chunk whose exit_code is a non-zero integer, where the same cmd string is never seen again in that session with exit_code 0. This is the Claude scanner's rule ported to a harness that records the integer instead of a boolean, so the same GATE ranking and the same timeout exclusion apply unchanged.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: Codex writes the literal process exit code into the tool output; nothing in the pipeline interprets it or narrates it. The command string is read from custom_tool_call.input, which is the program the harness actually executed, not a description of what it meant to run. No assistant prose is consulted, matching the standard session_intake.py already holds.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes. The cmd string re-runs verbatim in turn_context.cwd. Acceptance test: run that exact command in that directory and require exit 0, with the recorded failing output attached so the night's work can be checked against what actually printed.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: The exec input is a JS program, often batching several commands through Promise.allSettled, so a whole-input regex attributes the failure to the wrong sub-command — parse the per-chunk label/exit_code pairs and map each back to its own cmd:. Search tools poison the signal: rg/grep/git grep exit 1 on 'no match', which is a normal result, and one observed chunk carried exit_code 5 on output that was a document. Drop commands whose first word is rg, grep, git grep, or diff.

intake_sources.name: doc_command_drift
intake_sources.what_it_reads: Fenced bash/sh/console blocks in README.md (12 fences here), CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md and docs/**/*.md, plus the run: blocks of .github/workflows/ci.yml. The repository already ships tools/check_readme_quickstart.py, which runs the README journey against the public CLI in a pinned container image — extend that file rather than write a second one beside it.
intake_sources.signal: A command the project publishes to strangers that exits non-zero when run in a fresh clone of HEAD. A broken quickstart is a defect with a known audience and a known cost, which is what separates it from a lint finding nobody asked for.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: The command text is copied out of a committed file, executed, and its exit code read. There is no judgement about whether documentation is 'out of date' — it either runs or it does not, and the evidence is the exact command plus the exact text it printed.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes, by construction: the documented command is the acceptance test. Phrasing it that way also pins the fix — the command line as published must work, so editing the documentation to describe the breakage does not pass.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: Fenced blocks contain output samples, placeholders such as <YOUR_KEY>, and destructive or networked commands. Run only lines beginning with a known-safe prefix (python -m loop_engine, pip install -e, pytest, npm ci, npm test), inside a fresh `git clone` in a scratch directory, with no credentials in the environment, and skip any line containing <, $YOUR, curl, sudo, rm, or a redirect into a repository path. A command that requires a secret is not drift — it is untestable here, and must be dropped rather than reported as failing.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
rm -rf /tmp/fresh && git clone -q --no-hardlinks . /tmp/fresh && cd /tmp/fresh
awk '/^```(bash|sh|console)$/{c=1;next} /^```$/{c=0;next} c' README.md CONTRIBUTING.md $(ls docs/**/*.md 2>/dev/null) \
 | grep -vE '<|\$YOUR|curl |sudo |rm |^\s*#|>' \
 | grep -E '^(python -m loop_engine|pip install -e|pytest|npm (ci|test))' \
 | sort -u | while IFS= read -r cmd; do
     timeout 300 env PYTHONPATH=src bash -c "$cmd" >/tmp/doc.log 2>&1
     rc=$?; [ $rc -eq 0 ] && continue; [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { echo "UNKNOWN(timeout) $cmd"; continue; }
     echo "DOC_DRIFT rc=$rc :: $cmd"; tail -5 /tmp/doc.log
   done

intake_sources.name: head_gate_red
intake_sources.what_it_reads: The gates the repository itself declares: the run: blocks in .github/workflows/ci.yml and the entry points in pyproject.toml. Concretely here — `python -m loop_engine --self-test`, `python -m loop_engine --conformance`, `cd devtools/qualification_lab && python -m unittest -v test_runner.py`, and the four examples/*/run.py invocations from the 'Examples run' step. Executed at HEAD in a throwaway `git worktree add`.
intake_sources.signal: A non-zero exit at a commit nobody touched today. This source needs no history at all: it asks the repository what is broken right now and reads the answer.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: You run the command and read its exit code and its real output. There is no transcript, no attribution, no claim to discount. This is the same evidence standard the existing tool applies to transcript commands, obtained first-hand instead of second-hand.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes — the candidate and its acceptance test are the same command, which makes it the cheapest source to verify and the hardest to fake a fix for. The empty answer is legible and must be reported as such: every gate exits 0, no candidates, and a night spent inventing one is worse than a night idle.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: An unconfigured local environment reports the machine broken rather than the code. Build a throwaway venv with `pip install -e '.[all]'` and only report gates that were red inside it. Timing is a real hazard: `--conformance` finished here in under 100 s with exit 0 ('ALL GATES PASS'), but `--self-test` did not finish inside a 120 s budget and CI's suite job takes about 4 minutes. Use a per-gate timeout of at least 400 s and record a timeout as UNKNOWN, never as failing — the existing scanner already refuses to build candidates from timeouts and this source must not undo that.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
python3 -m venv /tmp/gate && /tmp/gate/bin/pip install -q -e '.[all]'
git worktree add -d /tmp/head HEAD
while IFS= read -r g; do
  ( cd /tmp/head && timeout 400 env PATH=/tmp/gate/bin:$PATH bash -c "$g" ) >/tmp/out 2>&1
  rc=$?
  case $rc in
    0)   ;;
    124) echo "UNKNOWN(timeout 400s) $g" ;;
    *)   echo "RED(exit $rc) $g"; tail -20 /tmp/out ;;
  esac
done <<'GATES'
python -m loop_engine --self-test
python -m loop_engine --conformance
cd devtools/qualification_lab && python -m unittest test_runner.py
GATES

intake_sources.name: suppression_marker
intake_sources.what_it_reads: `git grep -n` over tracked sources for markers that instruct a checker to look away: `# type: ignore`, `# noqa:<CODE>`, `# pragma: no cover`, `@pytest.mark.xfail`, `@pytest.mark.skip`, `@unittest.skip`, `eslint-disable`, `@ts-expect-error`, `it.skip(`, `xit(`, `#[allow(dead_code)]`. Measured in this repository: 24 `type: ignore`, 79 `noqa`, 8 `pragma: no cover`, and zero xfail, skip, eslint-disable or ts-expect-error.
intake_sources.signal: A suppression is a gate someone switched off because they could not make it pass. Rank by how long the line has survived: `git log -1 -L <line>,<line>:<file>` gives the last commit that touched it, and a suppression nobody has revisited in months is one nobody intends to remove on their own.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: This is the defensible form of 'read the repository's TODO comments'. A bare TODO is a stated intention and fails the standard the existing tool set — it asserts an outcome nothing verified, which is exactly why session_intake.py already ranks the engineer's deferral wording last. A suppression is different in kind: it is a machine-readable instruction to a specific checker, and that checker will state precisely what was being hidden the moment the marker is deleted. Worth noting concretely: this repository contains 3 TODO/FIXME strings in all tracked Python, and two of them are session_intake.py's own regex, so a TODO-based source would return nothing here but its own reflection.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes, and it is free. Delete one marker and run the checker it names — `# noqa: F841` becomes `ruff check --select F841 <file>`, `xfail` becomes `pytest <nodeid>`, `# type: ignore` becomes mypy or pyright on that file. Acceptance test: the file passes that checker with the marker removed. The empty answer is real and worth reporting: if the checker still passes, the suppression was stale and deleting it is the entire change.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: Neither mypy nor pyright is installed on this machine (`command -v` returns nothing for both), so `# type: ignore` candidates cannot be verified here — and a candidate whose gate cannot run must be dropped, not proposed with a promise to install a tool overnight. A bare `# noqa` with no rule code is unresolvable, since you cannot tell which rule it silenced; require a code. And scope matters enormously: `ruff check src/ tools/` reports 1664 errors under this repository's current settings while `ruff check --select F821 src/ tools/` reports none, so never propose 'fix the lint' — propose exactly one rule code with a countable, currently non-zero violation set.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
git grep -nE '# *(type: ignore|noqa)(\[|: *)[A-Z]+[0-9]+|@pytest\.mark\.(xfail|skip)|@ts-expect-error' \
  -- '*.py' '*.ts' '*.mjs' | while IFS=: read -r f l rest; do
    code=$(printf '%s' "$rest" | grep -oE '[A-Z]+[0-9]+' | head -1)
    [ -z "$code" ] && continue          # bare noqa: cannot name a gate, drop it
    age=$(git log -1 --format=%cr -L "$l,$l:$f" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
    echo "$f:$l rule=$code last-touched=$age"
  done | sort -t= -k2
# verify one candidate: strip the marker on that line, then
#   ruff check --select "$code" "$f"    -- must exit 0 for the candidate to be real

intake_sources.name: worktree_delta
intake_sources.what_it_reads: `git status --porcelain` and `git diff --name-only HEAD` in every repository the day's sessions named — cwd from the Claude transcript records, payload.turn_context.cwd from the Codex rollouts. Verified in this checkout: 4 porcelain entries, of which two are tracked modifications (src/loop_engine/core/opencode_step_composition.py and src/loop_engine/core/opencode_step_composition_checks.py) and two are untracked files (gantt.html, test_output.txt).
intake_sources.signal: A declared gate that exits 0 in a clean `git worktree add` of HEAD and non-zero in a copy of the dirty working tree. That is a change in progress which broke something, caught before it was committed and before CI would ever see it.
intake_sources.why_observed_not_inferred: Two runs of one command against two trees, with both exit codes read directly. The claim 'this edit broke that gate' is a measured difference between two observations, not an attribution. Nothing is read from what anyone said they were doing.
intake_sources.gate_command: Yes, and it is unusually strong. The acceptance test is: the same gate now exits 0 with the working-tree changes still applied. Stating it that way forbids the lazy fix of reverting the engineer's work to make the gate green, which is the failure mode an overnight agent will otherwise reach for first.
intake_sources.false_positive_risk: The dirty tree may be a deliberate mid-refactor the engineer intends to finish in the morning, and an agent editing those same files overnight creates a merge conflict with a human. Copy the dirty tree to a scratch directory and work only there; never edit the live worktree. Restrict to tracked, modified files — untracked build junk like test_output.txt and gantt.html here is output, not work in progress. If the gate is already red at clean HEAD, this source yields nothing and the candidate belongs to head_gate_red instead.
intake_sources.detection_sketch:
dirty=$(git diff --name-only HEAD -- '*.py'); [ -z "$dirty" ] && exit 0
git worktree add -d /tmp/clean HEAD
gate="python -m loop_engine --self-test"
( cd /tmp/clean && timeout 400 env PYTHONPATH=src bash -c "$gate" ) >/dev/null 2>&1; clean=$?
rm -rf /tmp/scratch && cp -a . /tmp/scratch
( cd /tmp/scratch && timeout 400 env PYTHONPATH=src bash -c "$gate" ) >/tmp/dirty.log 2>&1; dirtyrc=$?
if [ $clean -eq 0 ] && [ $dirtyrc -ne 0 ] && [ $dirtyrc -ne 124 ]; then
  echo "worktree_delta: '$gate' green at HEAD, exit $dirtyrc with $dirty"; tail -20 /tmp/dirty.log
fi
